'''Michael J. T. Guy''' (born 1 April 1943{{citation needed|date=March 2020}}) is a British [[computer scientist]] and [[mathematician]]. He is known for early work on computer systems, such as the [[Phoenix (computer)|Phoenix]] system at the [[University of Cambridge]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.michaelgrant.dsl.pipex.com/phx.html |title=Archived copy |access-date=22 March 2008 |archive-date=21 February 2007 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070221071500/http://www.michaelgrant.dsl.pipex.com/phx.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> and for contributions to [[number theory]], [[computer algebra]], and the theory of [[polyhedra]] in higher dimensions. He worked closely with [[John Horton Conway]], and is the son of Conway's collaborator [[Richard K. Guy]].

== Mathematical work ==
With [[John Horton Conway|Conway]], Guy found the complete solution to the [[Soma cube]] of [[Piet Hein (scientist)|Piet Hein]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Weisstein |first=Eric W. |date=<!-- Undated --> |url=https://mathworld.wolfram.com/SomaCube.html |title=Soma Cube |website=Wolfram MathWorld}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Kustes |first=William (Bill) |url=http://www.fam-bundgaard.dk/SOMA/NEWS/N030518.HTM |title=The SOMAP construction map |website=SOMA News}}</ref> Also with Conway, an enumeration led to the discovery of the [[grand antiprism]], an unusual [[uniform polychoron]] in four dimensions. The two had met at [[Gonville and Caius College, Cambridge]], where Guy was an undergraduate student from 1960, and Conway was a graduate student. It was through Michael that Conway met Richard Guy, who would become a co-author of works in [[combinatorial game theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Guy |first=Richard K. |title=[[John Horton Conway]]: Mathematical Magus |journal=The Two-Year College Mathematics Journal |volume=13 |issue=5 |date=November 1982 |pages=290–299|doi=10.2307/3026500 |jstor=3026500 }}</ref> Michael Guy with Conway made numerous particular contributions to geometry, number and game theory, often published in problem selections by Richard Guy. Some of these are [[recreational mathematics]], others contributions to [[discrete mathematics]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Conway |first1=J.H. |author-link=John Horton Conway |last2=Guy |first2=M. J. T. |date=1982 |title=Message graphs |journal=Annals of Discrete Mathematics |volume=13 |pages=61–64}}</ref> They also worked on the [[sporadic group]]s.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Griess |first=Robert L. Jr. |author-link=Robert Griess |date=1998 |title=Twelve Sporadic Groups |url=https://www.springer.com/gp/book/9783540627784 |location=[[New York City]] |publisher=Springer |page=127 |isbn=978-3-662-03516-0}}</ref>

Guy began work as a research student of [[J. W. S. Cassels]] at [[Faculty of Mathematics, University of Cambridge|Department of Pure Mathematics and Mathematical Statistics]] (DPMMS), Cambridge.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Cassels |first=J. W. S. |author-link=J. W. S. Cassels |date=1995 |title=Computer-aided serendipity |journal=Rendiconti del Seminario Matematico della Università di Padova |volume=93 |pages=187–197}}</ref> He did not complete a Ph.D., but joint work with Cassels produced numerical examples on the [[Hasse principle]] for [[cubic surface]]s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cassels |first1=J. W. S. |author-link=J. W. S. Cassels |last2=Guy |first2=M. J. T. |date=1966 |title=On the Hasse principle for cubic surfaces |journal=[[Mathematika]] |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=111–120|doi=10.1112/S0025579300003879 }}</ref>

== Computer science ==
He subsequently went into computer science. He worked on the [[file system|filing system]] for [[Titan (1963 computer)|Titan]], Cambridge's [[Atlas (computer)|Atlas 2]],<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Herbert |first1=Andrew J. |last2=Needham |first2=Roger Michael |last3=Spärck Jones |first3=Karen I. B. |date=2004 |title=Computer Systems: Theory, Technology, and Applications: a Tribute to [[Roger Needham]] |page=[https://archive.org/details/springer_10.1007-b97622/page/n109 105]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://elearn.cs.man.ac.uk/~atlas/docs/Atlas%202%20at%20Cambridge%20Mathematical%20Laboratory.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181125233855/https://elearn.cs.man.ac.uk/~atlas/docs/Atlas%202%20at%20Cambridge%20Mathematical%20Laboratory.pdf |archive-date=25 November 2018 | title=Atlas 2 at Cambridge Mathematical Laboratory (And Aldermaston and CAD Centre) | access-date=24 July 2020}}</ref> being one of a team of four in one office including [[Roger Needham]].<ref>{{Cite web |editor-last=Hartley |editor-first=David |date=21 July 1999 |url=http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/conference/EDSAC99/reminiscences/ |title=EDSAC 1 and after |website=Computer Laboratory |publisher=University of Cambridge}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last1=Wheeler |first1=David |last2=Hartley |first2=David |date=March 1999 |url=http://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/Relics/chron.html |title=Computer Laboratory - Events in the early history of the Computer Laboratory |website=Department of Computer Science and Technology |publisher=University of Cambridge}}</ref> In working on [[ALGOL 68]], he was co-author with [[Stephen R. Bourne]] of [[ALGOL 68C]].<ref>[http://hopl.murdoch.edu.au/showlanguage2.prx?exp=667 The Encyclopedia of Computer Languages<!-- Bot generated title -->] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20070825202944/http://hopl.murdoch.edu.au/showlanguage2.prx?exp=667 |date=25 August 2007 }}</ref><ref>[http://burks.bton.ac.uk/burks/foldoc/41/4.htm ALGOL 68C<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>
